title: Meta-memorization and memorization scaling laws in transformers
claim: The training data are random binary sequences with a heavy-tailed Zipfian repetition distribution, so repetition counts span orders of magnitude.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side: sequence bars left, log-log rank-frequency plot right
description: Two-panel figure. Panel a, on the left, shows four horizontal binary strips labeled Sequence 0 to Sequence 3. Each strip has dark navy and pale peach segments that mark random 0/1 bits, with no visible structure. Panel b, on the right, is titled 'Rank Frequency Distribution'. It is a log-log plot of Count (10^1 to 10^4) against Rank (10^0 to 10^3). Blue dots for the empirical counts lie along a straight orange line for the expected Zipfian power law. The scatter widens at high ranks. The legend sits at the top right. The dark bars in panel a draw the eye first, then the straight line in panel b. The overall look is clean and sparse.
caption: Experimental setup. We train autoregressive transformers on K = 105 random binary sequences of length N = 100. (a) Four example sequences. (b) Sequences are assigned ranks and sampled from a Zipfian distribution, producing repetition counts spanning orders of magnitude. For illustrative purposes we only plot up to rank 103. Model size is varied through the number of heads H and model dimension D.
abstract: Larger transformers can memorize more data, with a capacity (in bits) that scales roughly linearly with the number of parameters. Counterintuitively, larger models also memorize faster, requiring fewer repetitions of a sequence during training before it is memorized. We reproduce both memorization scaling laws in transformers trained on random binary sequences, showing that rapid memorization can arise even when data contain no semantic or compositional structure. Rapid memorization is due to a meta-memorization effect, where models trained to memorize a large set of random sequences learn to memorize novel sequences more quickly. The rate $r(t)$ at which models memorize grows with training time $t$ as a power-law $r(t) \sim t^Î²$ with a fixed exponent $Î²$ but an increasing upper cutoff across model scales. Meta-memorization enables even one-layer transformers to few-shot memorize a 100-bit sequence. This effect is partly explained by the formation of structured attention heads that convey position-invariant sequence information to MLPs where memorized sequences are stored. Meta-memorization is recapitulated in a simplified model of a dense associative memory where retrieval is constrained by an attentional bottleneck. Our results suggest transformers, through pre-training, acquire reusable mechanisms that enable highly efficient storage and retrieval of memories.
